notes: Brackets: the booklet prints one table for every filing status, on taxable nonbusiness income (IT 1040 line 7), columns 'More than' and 'Up to' (PDF p.18): 0 to 26,050, 0.000%; 26,050 to 100,000, '$ 342.00 plus 2.750% of the amount in excess of $ 26,050'; 100,000 and over, '$2,394.32 plus 3.125% of the amount in excess of $100,000'. So tax is 0 at exactly 26,050 and 342.00 and a fraction just above it, and the table steps up at both thresholds. Single and married_joint carry the same list; no separate married separate or head of household schedule is printed.

Printed lump sums: each band above the first carries the printed amount in `base` (342.00 at 26,050; 2,394.32 at 100,000), so tax above the start is the base plus the rate on the excess, as the table prints it. brackets.derivation re-checks printed rows and the booklet's worked example.

Printed table is not continuous at 100,000: 342 + 2.75% x 73,950 is 2,375.63 at the top of the second band, and the third band starts from the printed 2,394.32, 18.70 higher. Taken as printed; no second table is in the sources (the Department's tax.ohio.gov/taxcalculator tool is not archived). The booklet's letter (PDF p.4) says 'Ohio has lowered the tax rate applied to taxable nonbusiness income above $100,000 to 3.125%'. Worked example PDF p.18: 68,050 gives 342 + 42,000 x 0.0275 = 1,497.

brackets.derivation.formula is left out: that field holds 'rate x income minus constant', and the constants this table implies (374.375, 730.68) are not printed, so the printed base-plus-rate formulas are held in the notes above and proved by the table_rows. Row incomes 26,051 and 100,001 are the first whole dollars over each threshold, where the printed bases 342.00 and 2,394.32 are the row figures to within 0.04.

Returns are in whole dollars ('Round all figures to the nearest dollar', PDF p.5; 'Round numbers to the nearest dollar', PDF p.7); the bands above are exact to the cent, so they hold for rounded figures too.

Ohio starts from federal AGI (IT 1040 line 1), adds and deducts on the Ohio Schedule of Adjustments, then line 3 Ohio AGI less line 4 exemptions is line 5, the Ohio income tax base; line 6 taxable business income comes off to give line 7, taxable nonbusiness income, the bracket base (bundle PDF p.1).

The booklet prints no standard deduction. The exemption (line 4) is the only personal allowance; no age-65 or blindness amount is printed. Example PDF p.17: three exemptions at MAGI 75,000 total 6,450 (3 x 2,150).

Pension from another state's government, including a New York State pension: no source names one, and none treats it apart from other retirement income, so it falls under the general rule. Department FAQ 5: 'A state can only tax the retirement income of a resident taxpayer. Thus, if an Ohio resident earns or receives retirement income, it is subject to tax in Ohio even if the taxpayer previously lived or worked in another state. This includes any amount included in the taxpayer's federal adjusted gross income.' FAQ 1: 'Generally, retirement income included in federal adjusted gross income is subject to Ohio income tax. Ohio then provides a credit based on the taxpayer's retirement income.' FAQ 3 lists the only deductible kinds (Social Security and tier I railroad, certain other railroad, retired military pay). So a New York State pension is taxed in full, and counts toward the retirement income credit, which covers income from 'a pension, profit-sharing, or retirement plan' whoever pays it (public_pension_other_state in that entry's covers). No paying_states: no rule turns on which state pays.

Ohio's own and federal government pensions: no deduction is printed, the same rule applies, and they are in the retirement income credit's covers without being named: Senior Citizens page: 'Other retirement income included in your Ohio adjusted gross income is usually taxed by Ohio, but you may qualify for credits like Ohio's retirement income credit or the lump sum retirement credit.' The one exception is the military-years share of a federal civil service pension (line 34, federal_civil_service_military_share).
Private pensions, IRAs, 401(k) plans: taxed, same FAQ 1 sentence; retirement income credit only ('such as traditional IRAs or 401(k) plans', PDF p.28).

Roth conversions: FAQ 8: 'if your rollover results in recognizing income that is included in your federal adjusted gross income (e.g. converting to a Roth IRA), it will be taxable to Ohio.' So a conversion is taxed. Whether it counts toward the retirement income credit is not settled: the credit needs income received 'on account of retirement', and FAQ 7 says 'Early withdraws and distributions do not qualify for this credit'; hence covers_unclear.

Social Security: exempt. Senior Citizens page: 'Ohio does not tax Social Security benefits.' Booklet PDF p.20, Schedule of Adjustments line 16: 'Deduct the amount on your federal 1040 or 1040-SR, line 6b.' Same line on bundle PDF p.3. Filing tip on the Senior Citizens page: if the taxable amount exceeds federal AGI, deduct only up to federal AGI.

Retirement income credit table (PDF p.44 Table 2; FAQ 2 prints the same table): 0-500: 0; 501-1,500: 25; 1,501-3,000: 50; 3,001-5,000: 80; 5,001-8,000: 130; 8,001 or more: 200. It steps on the eligible retirement income itself, while the schema's stepped income_test takes one measure and that slot holds the 100,000 test, so the table is in cap_rule.

Senior citizen credit: PDF p.28 says 'You were 65 or older at the end of the tax year' and 'The credit is equal to $50 per return'; FAQ 2 says 'Taxpayers who were 65 or older during the tax year'. Bundle PDF p.7 line 4: 'must be 65 or older to claim this credit'. Neither says how a joint return with one spouse 65 is tested.
The credits recorded here (Schedule of Credits lines 2, 3, 4, 5, 9 and 12) come under the 'Nonrefundable Credits' heading (PDF p.28); line 11 says 'if negative, enter zero'.

Credits and deductions not given entries: earned income credit, 30% of the federal credit (PDF p.30); child and dependent care credit (PDF p.28); Ohio resident credit for tax paid to another state (PDF p.40); displaced worker, campaign contribution and home school credits. Unreimbursed medical deduction (line 44, PDF pp.25, 41): premiums for periods without Medicare or an employer plan and long-term care premiums in full, plus Medicare-period premiums and medical care over 7.5% of federal AGI; no entry because it is not tied to an income kind and premiums are not a yearly fact.

Business income (PDF pp.11, 27; bundle PDF p.5 lines 11 to 16): 'Taxpayers can deduct the first $250,000 ($125,000 for married separate filers) of their business income included in their federal adjusted gross income. Also, any business income not deducted is taxed at a flat 3%.' The 3% is a separate tax on line 6, not a bracket; the schema has no field for it, so it is in the business_income_deduction entry's cap_rule. The deduction is added back in MAGI.

Interest: non-Ohio state and local obligations are added (line 1, PDF p.19); Ohio public obligations are deducted (line 18, PDF pp.20-21); U.S. obligations exempt by federal law, such as savings bonds and Treasury notes, bills and bonds, are deducted (line 26, PDF p.22).
Not stated in any source: a capital gains rate or exclusion for nonbusiness gains (they run through the brackets); inflation adjustment of any figure. Recapture: none found.

School district income tax (SD 100) is a local tax, not recorded. Senior Citizens page: 'Neither tax base includes Social Security income, and retirement income is only taxed in traditional tax base districts.'
